blocks.source: Vol III, Durable Execution, § Recorded Trajectory Replay
blocks.md: When an agent execution stalls or fails during an automated repair, resuming the session admits fresh work under current system conditions. Post-mortem debugging asks a different question, namely what the runtime recorded at the moment of failure and how the harness code responded to the inputs available at that time. Rerunning a targeted test like `test_r18` under a new attempt cannot resolve that inquiry. Because external services drift, package versions change, and model sampling introduces variance, a new execution merely supplies fresh observations rather than reproducing the missing historical outcome.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Projection reconstruction
- Harness regression replay
- Counterfactual branches

questions.q: The section **Recorded Trajectory Replay** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: An admitted operation's identity, arguments, grant reference, and reservation must be durable under the declared failure domain before the request leaves, so no effect can exist without its intent on record.
Resume is an authorized continuation in ordered stages (prove the prefix, acquire ownership with a fencing epoch, restore by fold, reconcile in-doubt operations) rather than a restart.

Young's interval prices checkpoints when a crash loses work to re-execute, and once each turn is logged the stride lengthens by the square root of the cost ratio because a crash costs reconstruction, not resampling.

A sampled model reply cannot be regenerated, so reproduction substitutes recorded inputs at nondeterministic boundaries, and one recording serves time-travel inspection, harness regression, and counterfactual branching.
